*Core insight / definition:* Decomposition splits a series into trend (long-term direction), seasonality (repeating periodic pattern), and residual/remainder (irregular component), either additively (`y = trend + seasonal + resid`) or multiplicatively. STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess) performs this decomposition robustly using local regression, handling changing seasonality over time better than classical fixed decomposition.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Choosing additive vs. multiplicative decomposition incorrectly (e.g., additive when seasonal amplitude actually grows with the trend level) produces a poorly-fitting decomposition — interviewers may show a plot and ask which to use.

---

**SentencePiece / BPE / WordPiece (Subword Tokenization)**

*The problem:* Word-level tokenization has an unbounded, sparse vocabulary and fails on unseen words; character-level tokenization avoids OOV but produces very long sequences and weak per-token semantics.

*Core insight / definition:* Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs into new subword units, building a fixed-size vocabulary that balances sequence length and OOV robustness. WordPiece is a similar merge-based algorithm (used by BERT) that instead selects merges maximizing training-data likelihood. SentencePiece treats the input as a raw stream (including spaces) and applies BPE or unigram-language-model tokenization directly, making it language-agnostic (no whitespace-based pre-tokenization required).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* SentencePiece's whitespace-agnostic design is specifically what makes it work well for languages without clear word boundaries (e.g., Japanese, Chinese) — a detail interviewers use to test if you understand why different LLMs pick different tokenizers.

---

**Stemming / Lemmatization**

*The problem:* Text often contains many surface forms of the same underlying word (run, running, ran), which can fragment vocabulary and hurt statistical text representations unless normalized.

*Core insight / definition:* Stemming crudely chops word endings using fixed heuristic rules to reach a root form (which may not be a real word, e.g., "running" → "runn"); lemmatization uses vocabulary and morphological/grammatical analysis to map a word to its proper dictionary base form (lemma), e.g., "ran" → "run," and is more linguistically accurate but slower.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Stemming can conflate unrelated words or produce non-words, so lemmatization is preferred when interpretability of normalized tokens matters — a tradeoff interviewers ask you to weigh against stemming's speed advantage.

---

**STL** — *(see Seasonality Decomposition)*

---

**Swin Transformer**

*The problem:* Plain ViT computes global self-attention across all patches, which scales quadratically with image size/resolution and lacks the hierarchical, multi-scale feature pyramids that CNNs naturally provide for dense prediction tasks (detection, segmentation).

*Core insight / definition:* Swin Transformer computes self-attention within local, non-overlapping windows (reducing complexity to linear in image size) and shifts the window partitioning between successive layers to allow cross-window information flow, while progressively merging patches across stages to build a hierarchical, multi-resolution feature representation similar to CNNs.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* The shifted-window mechanism is the specific fix for windowed attention's lack of cross-window interaction — a common follow-up after explaining the windowing itself.

---

**SwiGLU**

*The problem:* Standard Transformer feed-forward blocks use a simple ReLU or GELU activation between two linear layers, which may limit the FFN's expressive gating capacity.

*Core insight / definition:* SwiGLU replaces the standard FFN activation with a gated linear unit variant using the Swish (SiLU) activation — computing an element-wise product of a linear projection and a Swish-activated linear projection — which empirically improves model quality at equivalent parameter count.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* SwiGLU's adoption (Llama, PaLM) is an empirically-motivated architecture choice, and interviewers may ask you to note that it typically requires adjusting the hidden dimension to keep parameter count comparable to a standard FFN.

---

**TBATS**

*The problem:* Series with multiple, possibly non-integer-period seasonalities (e.g., daily data with both weekly and yearly patterns) are hard to model with classical single-seasonality SARIMA.

*Core insight / definition:* TBATS (Trigonometric seasonality, Box-Cox transformation, ARMA errors, Trend, Seasonal components) models multiple seasonal periods simultaneously using trigonometric (Fourier-like) terms within a state-space framework, plus a Box-Cox transform for variance stabilization.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* It's one of several valid approaches to multi-seasonality (alongside Prophet and manual Fourier features) — interviewers testing this topic want you to name multiple options and their tradeoffs, not just one.

---

**TCN (Temporal Convolutional Network)**

*The problem:* RNNs process sequences step-by-step, which is slow to train (no parallelism across time) and can still struggle with very long-range dependencies despite gating mechanisms.

*Core insight / definition:* TCNs use causal, dilated 1D convolutions (convolutions that only look at past inputs, with dilation increasing receptive field exponentially with depth) to model sequences, enabling full parallelism during training while still being able to reach long effective context via stacked dilated layers.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Causality (no future leakage) must be enforced by construction (padding/masking), and interviewers may ask how dilation rate is chosen to cover a target receptive field length.

---

**Teacher Forcing** — *(see Exposure Bias / Teacher Forcing)*

---

**Text Classification (NLP)**

*The problem:* Many practical NLP tasks (sentiment analysis, spam detection, topic labeling) reduce to assigning a document or sentence to one or more predefined categories.

*Core insight / definition:* Text classification maps an input text to a label (or set of labels) using a trained model, ranging from classical approaches (TF-IDF + logistic regression/SVM) to fine-tuned pretrained transformer encoders (BERT with a classification head), with model choice depending on data volume, latency needs, and required accuracy.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* A common pitfall is applying only accuracy as the metric on imbalanced classification datasets (e.g., spam detection), when precision/recall/F1 or PR-AUC are usually more appropriate.

---

**TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency)**

*The problem:* Raw word counts (bag-of-words) overweight common but uninformative words (e.g., "the," "is") that appear in nearly every document, diluting the signal from more distinctive, informative words.

*Core insight / definition:* TF-IDF weights each word's count in a document (term frequency) by the inverse of how many documents in the corpus contain that word (inverse document frequency), so words common across the whole corpus are downweighted while words distinctive to a given document are upweighted.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* TF-IDF still ignores word order and semantics — a classical baseline interviewers ask you to compare against embeddings, especially on the question "why would you ever still use TF-IDF over embeddings?" (interpretability, speed, no training needed).

---

**Time Series Cross-Validation** — *(see Cross-Validation for Time Series)*

---

**TimeGPT-1 / Chronos / Lag-Llama / Moirai / TimesFM (Time Series Foundation Models)**

*The problem:* Every forecasting project traditionally starts from scratch — collecting data, engineering features, and training a model — which is infeasible at scale (tens of thousands of series) or with very limited history for a new series.

*Core insight / definition:* Foundation models for time series are pretrained on massive, diverse corpora of time series and can forecast new series zero-shot at inference without retraining. TimeGPT-1 (Nixtla) is API-based and transformer-based; Chronos (Amazon) quantizes numeric values into discrete tokens and applies a T5-style language model to autoregressively generate forecast tokens; Lag-Llama uses a Llama-style decoder-only transformer with patch tokenization; Moirai (Salesforce) uses a masked encoder handling variable context/prediction lengths and variable counts; TimesFM (Google) is a decoder-only autoregressive patching model.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Chronos's quantization introduces discretization error that loses very fine-grained (sub-0.1%) signal changes; more broadly, zero-shot foundation-model performance often lags fine-tuned task-specific models when ample task-specific data is actually available — know when NOT to reach for a foundation model.

---

**Tokenization (Word / Character / Subword)**

*The problem:* Raw text must be split into discrete units before any numerical model can process it, and the granularity of this split has major consequences for vocabulary size, OOV handling, and sequence length.

*Core insight / definition:* Word-level tokenization splits on whitespace/punctuation, giving intuitive units but an unbounded vocabulary and OOV problems. Character-level tokenization uses individual characters, giving a tiny vocabulary and no OOV issue but very long sequences and weak per-token meaning. Subword tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) is the modern middle ground, balancing vocabulary size, sequence length, and OOV robustness.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* This word/character/subword tradeoff is the near-universal opening question in NLP interviews — expect to justify why virtually all modern LLMs use subword tokenization.

---

**U-Net**

*The problem:* Segmentation, especially in domains with limited training data (e.g., biomedical imaging), needs an architecture that produces precise, high-resolution pixel-level output while still capturing broad contextual information.

*Core insight / definition:* U-Net uses a symmetric encoder-decoder ("U-shaped") architecture where the decoder path is connected to corresponding encoder layers via skip connections, which pass high-resolution spatial detail directly to the decoder, restoring fine boundary detail lost during downsampling.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* The skip connections (concatenating encoder features into the decoder) are the specific fix for the resolution loss that plain FCN upsampling suffers from — a direct architecture-comparison question.

---

**VAR (Vector Autoregression)**

*The problem:* Univariate forecasting models ignore potentially useful information from other correlated time series when multiple related series are being forecast simultaneously.

*Core insight / definition:* VAR models multiple time series jointly, where each series is regressed on its own past values and the past values of all other series in the system, capturing linear cross-series (Granger-causal-style) dependencies.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* VAR's parameter count grows quadratically with the number of series, so it becomes impractical (overfits) at high dimensionality — this scaling limitation is a common contrast point against global deep learning models.

---

**ViT (Vision Transformer) / DeiT**

*The problem:* CNNs bake in strong inductive biases (locality, translation equivariance) via convolution; researchers wanted to test whether a pure Transformer, with far weaker built-in visual assumptions, could match or exceed CNN performance given enough data.

*Core insight / definition:* ViT splits an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embeds each as a token (plus a learnable [CLS] token and positional embeddings), and processes the sequence with a standard Transformer encoder, treating image classification as a sequence-modeling problem; because it lacks convolution's built-in locality bias, it requires large-scale pretraining data to match CNN performance. DeiT introduces a distillation token and training recipe that lets ViT-style models train effectively on much smaller datasets (e.g., ImageNet-scale only) using a CNN teacher.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* "ViT lacks inductive bias, so it needs more data" is the headline fact, but DeiT's distillation-based fix for the data-hungry problem is the necessary follow-up interviewers look for.

---

**Word2Vec (Skip-gram / CBOW)**

*The problem:* Sparse, high-dimensional bag-of-words/TF-IDF representations don't capture semantic similarity between words (e.g., "king" and "queen" look unrelated as one-hot vectors).

*Core insight / definition:* Word2Vec learns dense, low-dimensional word embeddings by training a shallow neural network to predict context words from a target word (skip-gram) or a target word from its context (CBOW), such that words appearing in similar contexts end up with similar vectors — famously supporting analogy arithmetic like `king - man + woman ≈ queen`.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Word2Vec produces exactly one static vector per word regardless of context, so it cannot disambiguate polysemous words (e.g., "bank" the river vs. "bank" the institution) — the specific limitation that motivated contextual embeddings like ELMo and BERT.

---

**Word Embeddings — Contextual (ELMo, BERT) vs. Static (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText)**

*The problem:* Static embeddings assign a fixed vector per word regardless of surrounding context, failing to capture polysemy (a word's meaning changing based on usage).

*Core insight / definition:* Static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText) produce one vector per word type, learned once from a large corpus. Contextual embeddings (ELMo, using bidirectional LSTMs; BERT, using bidirectional Transformers) instead compute a different vector for each word occurrence based on its surrounding sentence context, produced dynamically at inference time by the full model.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Interviewers use polysemy ("bank," "bat") as the standard example to test whether you understand exactly why contextual embeddings represented a major leap over static ones, not just that they're "better."

---

**YOLO (You Only Look Once) / SSD**

*The problem:* Two-stage detectors' separate proposal-then-classify pipeline is too slow for real-time detection applications (video, robotics).

*Core insight / definition:* YOLO and SSD are one-stage detectors that directly predict bounding boxes and class probabilities from a dense grid of spatial locations (and anchors) in a single forward pass through the network, trading some accuracy (especially on small/overlapping objects) for large gains in inference speed, enabling real-time detection.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Early YOLO versions struggled with small and closely-packed objects due to the coarse grid — a known limitation that later YOLO versions and anchor/focal-loss refinements addressed, worth mentioning if asked about YOLO's weaknesses.

---

**Z-score (Anomaly Detection)**

*The problem:* Detecting whether a single observation is anomalous requires a simple, interpretable measure of how far it deviates from typical/expected behavior.

*Core insight / definition:* The Z-score standardizes a value by subtracting the (local or global) mean and dividing by the standard deviation, flagging points beyond a chosen threshold (e.g., |Z| > 3) as anomalies.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Applying Z-score directly to raw seasonal data flags legitimate seasonal peaks as false anomalies; it should be computed on deseasonalized/detrended residuals — a frequently tested pitfall.

---


## 08-generative

**Anomaly Detection (via generative models)**

*The problem:* you need to flag inputs that don't belong to the training distribution, without labeled anomaly examples.

*Core insight / definition:* train a generative model (autoencoder, flow) on normal data only; use reconstruction error or likelihood as an anomaly score — high error/low likelihood suggests out-of-distribution input.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* likelihood-based anomaly detection is pathological for flows and deep generative models — they can assign higher likelihood to simpler/smoother out-of-distribution inputs (e.g., flows trained on CIFAR-10 rate SVHN higher) regardless of semantic distribution membership; this is not fixed by more training or a bigger model.

---

**Autoregressive Model**

*The problem:* you want exact likelihood without requiring an invertible, dimension-preserving architecture like flows demand.

*Core insight / definition:* factor the joint distribution exactly via the chain rule, $p_\theta(x) = \prod_{i=1}^{d} p_\theta(x_i \mid x_{<i})$, where each conditional is a tractable 1-D distribution (softmax over pixels/tokens). The product recovers the exact joint likelihood with no approximation.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* training is parallel (teacher forcing, one forward pass with causal masking) but sampling is inherently sequential ($d$ passes) because each $x_i$ requires $x_{<i}$ to exist — this asymmetry is the chain-rule factorization's property, not an architecture quirk, and applies identically to LLMs (next-token prediction is exactly this).

---

**β-VAE**

*The problem:* standard VAEs don't reliably produce disentangled, interpretable latent dimensions.

*Core insight / definition:* multiply the KL term in the ELBO by $\beta > 1$: $\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \beta \cdot D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)\|p(z))$. Higher $\beta$ pushes the latent space to be smoother and more disentangled, with dimensions tending to align with independent generative factors (pose, color, shape).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* increasing $\beta$ trades away reconstruction quality — too high causes posterior collapse for the opposite reason of the standard failure (KL pressure dominates before the decoder learns to use $z$); the fix for collapse depends on whether it's decoder-driven or KL-driven, and reaching for β-VAE without diagnosing which is a common trap.

---

**BERT / Masked Language Modeling (as denoising autoencoder)**

*The problem:* illustrating that denoising autoencoding is a general training paradigm, not just an image technique.

*Core insight / definition:* BERT's masked language modeling is structurally a denoising autoencoder — mask some tokens (corruption), predict the original tokens (reconstruction) — the same objective pattern applied to text.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* recognizing this connection signals a deeper understanding of generative/self-supervised objectives across modalities rather than treating each architecture as a special case.

---

**Change of Variables Formula**

*The problem:* to get an exact density under an invertible transformation of a simple base distribution, you need a way to account for how the transformation distorts volume.

*Core insight / definition:* for $x = f_\theta(z)$ with $z \sim p_Z$, $\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z(f_\theta^{-1}(x)) + \log|\det \partial f_\theta^{-1}/\partial x|$ — an equality, not a bound, that lets normalizing flows be trained by directly maximizing exact likelihood.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the Jacobian determinant is $O(d^3)$ for a general transform — fatal for high dimensions — so every flow architecture exists specifically to make this determinant cheap to compute.

---

**Classifier-Free Guidance**

*The problem:* diffusion models conditioned on text (or other signals) don't reliably follow the conditioning signal at generation time.

*Core insight / definition:* scale the difference between conditional and unconditional noise predictions by a guidance weight to trade diversity for fidelity/prompt adherence; works reliably in diffusion models because training is stable regression, unlike adversarial setups.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* too low a guidance weight yields plausible images with weak prompt adherence; too high oversaturates and collapses diversity — it's a fidelity/diversity dial, not a pure quality dial, and cannot fix compositional failures (counting, spatial relations) rooted in the text encoder or cross-attention conditioning.

---

**Consistency Distillation**

*The problem:* you want a fast consistency model but need an efficient way to define the ODE trajectories it must learn to shortcut.

*Core insight / definition:* start from an already-trained diffusion/flow model as a teacher; use it with a numerical ODE solver to generate adjacent points on trajectories, then train the consistency model $f_\theta$ to agree on nearby $(x_t, x_{t'})$ pairs from the same trajectory.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* distillation requires a pretrained teacher — calling any consistency model "a distilled diffusion model" is wrong when it was built via consistency *training* instead, which has no teacher.

---

**Consistency Model**

*The problem:* diffusion/flow sampling requires many sequential network evaluations (20-50+ steps), which dominates serving cost at scale; naively switching to a GAN reintroduces adversarial instability.

*Core insight / definition:* train a function $f_\theta$ such that any point on a diffusion/flow model's ODE trajectory maps to the same origin: $f_\theta(x_t, t) = f_\theta(x_{t'}, t') = x_0$ for any $t, t'$ on the same trajectory, with identity-consistency enforced at $t=0$. Sampling becomes a single call: draw noise, apply $f_\theta$, done.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* 1-step consistency models visibly lag multi-step diffusion on fine detail and diversity, so production systems typically land at 4-8 steps rather than 1; also, the sampling-time function is a direct trajectory-shortcut regressor, not an iterative denoiser — calling it "diffusion with fewer steps" undersells the structurally different training objective (self-consistency vs. per-step noise/velocity regression).

---

**Consistency Training**

*The problem:* consistency distillation depends on having a good pretrained teacher model, which may not always be available or optimal.

*Core insight / definition:* train a consistency model with the same self-consistency loss as distillation, but estimate the trajectory locally from the forward-noising process directly instead of using a teacher model.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* slower to converge and historically lower quality than consistency distillation, but removes the teacher dependency — this is the key distinguishing fact interviewers probe for.

---

**Coupling Layer (RealNVP)**

*The problem:* normalizing flows need an invertible transformation whose Jacobian determinant is cheap to compute, ruling out arbitrary neural network transforms.

*Core insight / definition:* split the input in half; leave one half untouched and transform the other half using scale/shift parameters computed from the untouched half: $y_{1:k}=x_{1:k}$, $y_{k+1:d}=x_{k+1:d}\odot\exp(s(x_{1:k}))+t(x_{1:k})$. The Jacobian is triangular so its determinant is just the product of the diagonal, giving linear-time computation, and inversion is trivial algebra (subtract $t$, divide by $\exp(s)$) since $s$ and $t$ never need inverting.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* stacking many coupling layers while permuting which half is frozen accumulates expressiveness; the key insight is that $s$ and $t$ can be arbitrary (non-invertible) neural networks because they only ever operate on the passthrough half.

---

**Denoising Autoencoder (DAE)**

*The problem:* an undercomplete autoencoder trained to reconstruct exactly can be gamed by memorizing training examples rather than learning generalizable structure, and is brittle to input noise at test time.

*Core insight / definition:* corrupt the input (Gaussian noise, masking) before encoding, then train the decoder to reconstruct the clean original: $L = \|x - g_\theta(f_\phi(\tilde{x}))\|^2$. This forces the encoder to learn the underlying clean signal rather than memorize corrupted inputs.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the corruption distribution used in training must match test-time corruption, or the model won't generalize (e.g., Gaussian noise training won't transfer to salt-and-pepper noise at deployment).

---

**Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM)**

*The problem:* DDPM's stochastic reverse process requires simulating all $T$ (typically 1000) steps, making inference slow.

*Core insight / definition:* reframe the reverse diffusion process as a deterministic ODE rather than a stochastic process, using the same trained model. Because it's an ODE, a numerical solver can take larger steps, allowing 10-50 steps with minimal quality loss.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* DDIM does not retrain or distill the model — it's purely a different sampling scheme on the same weights; determinism also gives a reproducible noise→image map, enabling coherent latent interpolation and editing.

---

**Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)**

*The problem:* GANs' adversarial min-max training is structurally unstable (mode collapse, vanishing gradients, oscillation) with no convergence guarantee.

*Core insight / definition:* define a forward process that adds Gaussian noise over $T$ steps, with a closed form $q(x_t|x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0, (1-\bar\alpha_t)I)$; train a network $\epsilon_\theta$ to predict the noise added at a randomly sampled timestep via simple regression: $\mathcal{L}_\text{simple} = \mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,\epsilon}[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon, t)\|^2]$.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the closed-form forward process is a *training*-time optimization (decouples training cost from $T$) — inference still must walk the (reverse) steps sequentially since the reverse process has no closed form; this asymmetry is why training is cheap but inference is slow.

---

**Diffusion Transformer (DiT)**

*The problem:* U-Net convolutional backbones don't scale as predictably with parameters/compute as transformers do elsewhere in deep learning.

*Core insight / definition:* patchify the (usually latent-space) input into tokens and process with a standard transformer block stack, conditioning via adaptive layer norm rather than U-Net-style feature concatenation. Used in production systems like SD3 and FLUX.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* DiT is a backbone/architecture choice, decoupled from the training objective (e.g., flow matching) — the two are often paired in practice (straighter rectified-flow trajectories reduce forward passes needed; DiT's scaling makes each pass more worth paying for) but are not logically coupled.

---

**Discriminator**

*The problem:* a GAN generator needs a training signal since there's no tractable likelihood to maximize directly.

*Core insight / definition:* a network $D$ trained to distinguish real data from generator outputs, serving as a learned, adaptive loss function for the generator; trained jointly and adversarially with the generator $G$.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* saying the discriminator merely "classifies real vs. fake" misses the point — its purpose is to supply a gradient signal where no likelihood exists; being the loss function is also the source of instability, since the loss surface moves while you descend it.

---

**Disentanglement (latent factors)**

*The problem:* raw latent dimensions in a VAE typically don't correspond to independent, human-interpretable generative factors.

*Core insight / definition:* with sufficient KL pressure (β-VAE), latent dimensions tend to align with independent generative factors of variation (pose, color, shape) rather than entangled combinations.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* disentanglement comes at the direct cost of reconstruction fidelity — it is a trade-off dial (via β), not a free improvement.

---

**Earth-Mover (Wasserstein) Distance**

*The problem:* the standard GAN's Jensen-Shannon-like objective provides poor or vanishing gradients when the generator and data distributions don't overlap.

*Core insight / definition:* the metric underlying WGAN's critic objective, measuring the minimal "cost" to transform one distribution into another; unlike KL/JS divergence, it remains meaningful (non-zero, smooth) even for non-overlapping distributions.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this is what structurally fixes the vanishing gradient problem in WGAN — it's not a training trick but a change in the underlying divergence being optimized.

---

**ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund)**

*The problem:* the true marginal likelihood $\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x|z)p(z)\,dz$ is intractable to compute directly for a VAE.

*Core insight / definition:* a tractable lower bound on the log-likelihood, decomposed into a reconstruction term and a KL regularization term: $\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)\|p(z))$. Maximizing the ELBO is the VAE training objective.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the ELBO is a *bound*, not the exact likelihood, and the gap to the true likelihood is unknown — so ELBO values are not trustworthy for comparing different models' fit to data (unlike flows' exact likelihood).

---

**Encoder / Decoder**

*The problem:* need a general vocabulary for the two halves of an autoencoding architecture.

*Core insight / definition:* the encoder $f_\phi$ maps input $x$ to a latent representation $z$; the decoder $g_\theta$ maps $z$ back to reconstructed input space. In a VAE the encoder outputs distribution parameters rather than a point.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the asymmetry in what encoder/decoder must learn (e.g., DAE encoder must denoise, VAE encoder must produce a distribution) is what differentiates the various autoencoder variants.

---

**Flow Matching**

*The problem:* DDPM's training objective was never designed directly around the ODE that its reverse process implies, and the implied trajectories end up curved, requiring many small integration steps.

*Core insight / definition:* define a probability path $p_t$ that continuously interpolates between data and noise distributions, and directly regress a velocity field $v_\theta$ that generates that path: $\mathcal{L}_\text{FM} = \mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,x_1}[\|v_\theta(x_t,t)-(x_1-x_0)\|^2]$, with $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$. This is a generalization of DDPM — DDPM's forward process is one specific (curved) probability path; flow matching lets you choose the path, and choosing a straight one buys sampling speed.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* flow matching is not a different model family from diffusion — it's a different parameterization of the same "reverse a data→noise process" idea; describing it as merely "faster diffusion" misses that the speed is a downstream consequence of the (straight) path choice, not an independent trick.

---

**Gated PixelCNN (blind-spot fix)**

*The problem:* PixelCNN's masked convolutions, enforcing causal raster order, create a "blind spot" in the receptive field that never sees certain valid context pixels.

*Core insight / definition:* uses two separate convolutional stacks (horizontal and vertical) to fix PixelCNN's blind-spot problem while preserving the causal ordering constraint.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* illustrates that enforcing autoregressive causal ordering via masked convolutions is not trivial — naive masking leaves gaps in the effective receptive field.

---

**Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)**

*The problem:* direct likelihood maximization is intractable for complex distributions like images because $p_\theta(x)$ cannot be evaluated in closed form for a neural generator.

*Core insight / definition:* replace the likelihood criterion with an adversarial one via a minimax game between a generator $G$ and discriminator $D$: $\min_G \max_D \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_\text{data}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))]$. At Nash equilibrium, $D(x)=0.5$ everywhere — the discriminator cannot distinguish real from generated samples.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* reliably reaching the Nash equilibrium is the unsolved problem — the minimax formulation has no convergence guarantee, which is the root cause of mode collapse, vanishing gradients, and oscillation; GANs still retain one edge over diffusion: single-step (one forward pass) inference, which matters for real-time/low-latency generation.

---

**Generator**

*The problem:* need a network that produces samples from the learned data distribution given random noise.

*Core insight / definition:* the network $G$ in a GAN that maps noise $z \sim p_z$ to generated samples $G(z)$, trained to fool the discriminator into classifying its outputs as real.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the generator has no direct access to real data or a likelihood signal — its only training signal is the discriminator's gradient, which is why discriminator quality/behavior directly determines training stability.

---

**Gumbel-Softmax**

*The problem:* the reparameterization trick works for Gaussian (and other exponential-family) latents but breaks down for discrete/categorical latent variables, where sampling has no useful gradient.

*Core insight / definition:* a specialized continuous relaxation/estimator that enables gradient-based training through discrete categorical sampling, used as an alternative to standard reparameterization for discrete latents.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* interviewers may probe whether you know reparameterization has limits — Gaussian-only naive application is a common oversight.

---

**Image Generation (VAE use case)**

*The problem:* need to produce novel synthetic examples resembling training data.

*Core insight / definition:* sample $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ from the VAE's latent prior and pass through the trained decoder to generate new examples.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* VAE-generated images tend to be blurrier than GAN or diffusion outputs due to the reconstruction loss averaging over multiple plausible pixel configurations — VAE's real strength is the structured latent space, not raw sample sharpness.

---

**Interpolation (latent space)**

*The problem:* want to generate smooth, semantically meaningful transitions between two inputs.

*Core insight / definition:* because a VAE's latent space is densely covered (thanks to the KL regularization toward a smooth prior), linear interpolation between two encoded points, when decoded, produces a semantically meaningful blend rather than garbage.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* plain (non-variational) autoencoders don't reliably support this since their latent space has "holes" — regions never seen during training that decode to nonsense.

---

**Jacobian Determinant (in flows)**

*The problem:* the change-of-variables formula requires computing $\log|\det \partial f_\theta^{-1}/\partial x|$, and a general $d\times d$ determinant costs $O(d^3)$ — intractable at scale.

*Core insight / definition:* the determinant of the transformation's Jacobian matrix, which quantifies the local volume distortion introduced by the invertible map; every flow architecture is designed to make this determinant cheap (e.g., triangular via coupling layers, reducing cost to linear time).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this cost is the central design constraint of all normalizing flow architectures — understanding why naive flows are infeasible hinges on recognizing this bottleneck.

---

**KL Divergence (regularization term)**

*The problem:* an autoencoder's latent space can develop narrow, non-overlapping per-input distributions (or arbitrary point encodings) that leave gaps a decoder was never trained to handle.

*Core insight / definition:* $D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x)\|p(z))$ penalizes the encoder's output distribution for deviating from the prior $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$; for Gaussian encoder/prior it has closed form $D_{KL} = -\frac12\sum_j(1+\log\sigma_j^2-\mu_j^2-\sigma_j^2)$.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this term is easy for the optimizer to drive to zero by ignoring the input entirely — the root mechanism behind posterior/KL collapse.

---

**KL Collapse / Posterior Collapse**

*The problem:* during VAE training the model can find a shortcut that minimizes loss while making the latent space useless.

*Core insight / definition:* the encoder learns to output a distribution matching the prior regardless of input (KL term → 0), and the decoder learns a fixed output independent of $z$ — the latent variable is effectively unused.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* reconstruction loss can look deceptively fine if the data has low diversity, so teams miss it; it's a valid (if useless) local optimum whenever the decoder is powerful enough to model $p(x)$ without conditioning on $z$ — fixes include KL annealing (ramping β from 0) or a weaker decoder, not just cranking β up (which causes collapse for the opposite reason).

---

**Latent Diffusion**

*The problem:* running the diffusion denoising process directly in pixel space (e.g., 512×512) is computationally expensive per step.

*Core insight / definition:* denoise in a compressed latent space (e.g., 64×64 instead of 512×512, via an autoencoder), reducing per-step cost by roughly 64×. Used in systems like Stable Diffusion.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this is one of the main levers (alongside DDIM and consistency models) that closed diffusion's speed disadvantage relative to GANs' single-step inference.

---

**Latent Space / Latent Variable**

*The problem:* need a compressed or structured intermediate representation that captures the essential generative factors of data.

*Core insight / definition:* the (usually lower-dimensional) space $z$ that an encoder maps inputs into, and from which a decoder/generator reconstructs or generates data; different generative model families structure this space very differently (compressed & smooth for VAE, unstructured for GAN, same-dimension-as-data for flows/diffusion, absent for pure autoregressive models).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* comparing generative model families often reduces to comparing what constraints each imposes on the latent space (dimensionality, smoothness, invertibility) and what that buys or costs.

---

**Lipschitz Constraint (1-Lipschitz critic)**

*The problem:* WGAN's critic objective is only theoretically valid (a true Wasserstein distance estimator) if the critic function is constrained to be 1-Lipschitz.

*Core insight / definition:* a constraint requiring the critic's output to change no faster than its input — enforced in WGAN-GP via a gradient penalty term $\mathbb{E}[(\|\nabla_{\hat x} D(\hat x)\|_2 - 1)^2]$ added to the loss.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this is what provides meaningful gradients even when generator and data distributions don't overlap at all, structurally solving vanishing gradients rather than patching around them.

---

**Mode Collapse**

*The problem:* a GAN generator can "cheat" the adversarial game without learning the true data diversity.

*Core insight / definition:* the generator converges to a small set of outputs that reliably fool the current discriminator, and diversity in generated samples disappears — while the loss curve can look fine.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* not detectable from loss curves alone — must track sample diversity directly; "train the discriminator less" is a common but wrong fix, since it just trades mode collapse for vanishing gradients — WGAN-GP addresses the underlying cause structurally. Diffusion models have no mechanism for mode collapse since each training step is an independent regression on a random noise level.

---

**Non-Saturating Loss**

*The problem:* when the discriminator becomes too accurate, $\log(1-D(G(z))) \approx 0$ and the generator's gradient vanishes, halting learning.

*Core insight / definition:* reformulate the generator's objective to maximize $\log D(G(z))$ instead of minimizing $\log(1-D(G(z)))$ — mathematically related but numerically well-behaved even when $D$ is confident.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this is the standard fix for vanishing generator gradients, distinct from WGAN's structural Lipschitz-based solution.

---

**Normalizing Flow**

*The problem:* need a generative model with exact (not bounded or absent) likelihood, for applications like anomaly detection, compression, or rigorous model comparison.

*Core insight / definition:* push a simple base density through an invertible neural network map $x = f_\theta(z)$; the change-of-variables formula gives the exact density of $x$. Every architectural choice (e.g., coupling layers) exists to make the Jacobian determinant tractable.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* flows are dimension-preserving by construction (no bottleneck/compression), which is the structural reason they lost the image-synthesis race to diffusion despite exact likelihood; also, exact likelihood does not imply good anomaly detection — flows notoriously assign higher likelihood to simpler out-of-distribution images (e.g., CIFAR-10-trained flow rating SVHN higher).

---

**Progressive Distillation**

*The problem:* want to reduce diffusion sampling steps but without a single-shot consistency objective.

*Core insight / definition:* repeatedly train a student model to do in $N/2$ steps what a teacher does in $N$ steps, then repeat, halving the step count each round.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* distinct from consistency models — it reaches few-step generation through a sequence of distillation rounds (more training runs, conceptually simpler) rather than a single self-consistency objective targeting arbitrary trajectory points; often used as one stage in a longer pipeline alongside consistency-style objectives.

---

**Rectified Flow / Reflow**

*The problem:* even flow matching with arbitrary interpolation paths can leave curved trajectories that need many integration steps.

*Core insight / definition:* the simplest form of flow matching, where the target velocity is the straight line from data to noise. "Reflow" further straightens paths by resampling the model's own generated pairs $(x_0, x_1)$ and retraining, since a model trained on its own outputs learns non-crossing (straighter) trajectories.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* straight-line paths are exactly integrable with far fewer steps than curved ones — this is the mechanistic reason rectified flow enables 1-8 step (sometimes 1-step) sampling after reflow/distillation, versus DDIM's 20-50.

---

**Reparameterization Trick**

*The problem:* training a VAE with gradient descent requires backpropagating through the stochastic sampling step $z \sim q_\phi(z|x)$, but sampling has no derivative with respect to $\mu$ or $\sigma$.

*Core insight / definition:* separate randomness from learned parameters by sampling noise from a fixed external distribution and deterministically transforming it: $z = \mu + \epsilon \odot \sigma$, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$. Gradients flow through $\mu$ and $\sigma$ normally; $\epsilon$ is a constant input with no gradient.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* works cleanly for Gaussian (and a few other exponential-family) distributions but breaks down for discrete latents (e.g., categorical), which require Gumbel-Softmax or other specialized estimators instead.

---

**Representation Learning (autoencoder use case)**

*The problem:* want reusable, informative features from unlabeled data for downstream supervised tasks.

*Core insight / definition:* pre-train an encoder unsupervised (via autoencoding), then fine-tune it on a downstream labeled task, leveraging the compressed representation as a feature extractor.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the value of the encoder depends on the bottleneck actually forcing informative compression rather than a near-identity mapping.

---

**Score Matching / Score Function**

*The problem:* diffusion models need an underlying mathematical object describing how to move samples from noise toward data.

*Core insight / definition:* the (implicit) gradient of the log-density that DDPM's noise-prediction objective is equivalent to estimating; described as the "underlying object" DDPM models implicitly, versus flow matching's explicit velocity field.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* DDPM, score-based SDEs, and flow matching are different parameterizations of the same underlying idea (learning to reverse a data→noise process) — conflating them as unrelated model families is a common mistake.

---

**Sparse Autoencoder**

*The problem:* want a large, interpretable latent space where features are disentangled and individually meaningful, rather than a maximally compressed dense code.

*Core insight / definition:* allow a wide latent space but penalize simultaneous non-zero activations via an $L_1$ penalty: $L = \|x-\hat x\|^2 + \lambda\|z\|_1$. This drives most activations to zero per input, so each input activates only a small, interpretable subset of features.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* too large a $\lambda$ collapses reconstruction quality (achieves sparsity by zeroing everything); too small makes the sparsity constraint ineffective — tuning requires monitoring both reconstruction error and average activation fraction. Used in interpretability research (e.g., Anthropic's work on LLM activations) because sparse, high-dimensional codes map more readily to human-interpretable concepts.

---

**Speculative Decoding**

*The problem:* autoregressive sampling is inherently sequential ($O(d)$), which is slow for long sequences like LLM generation.

*Core insight / definition:* a technique that trades exactness or extra compute for parallelism in generation, mentioned as one way around the sequential-sampling bottleneck of autoregressive models.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* illustrates that the sequential-sampling limitation of autoregressive models (including LLMs) is fundamental to the chain-rule factorization, not the specific architecture (Transformer vs. LSTM) — workarounds must trade something away.

---

**Teacher Forcing**

*The problem:* need an efficient way to train an autoregressive model without literally generating each token sequentially during training.

*Core insight / definition:* during training, feed the ground-truth prefix so all conditionals $p(x_i|x_{<i})$ can be evaluated simultaneously in a single forward pass with causal masking, rather than sequentially.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this is exactly why autoregressive training parallelizes while sampling does not — at sampling time no ground-truth prefix exists, so each token must be generated before conditioning on it.

---

**Temporal Attention / Consistency (video diffusion)**

*The problem:* denoising video frames independently produces flicker — objects subtly change identity frame to frame since each frame's denoising trajectory is an independent sample.

*Core insight / definition:* add temporal attention/convolution layers so the model attends across frames (not just within one), making denoising jointly consistent across a video clip rather than per-frame.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* treating video generation as "just diffusion with an extra dimension" is a trap — the training objective generalizes for free, but consistency across the temporal axis requires explicit architectural additions and compute strategies (chunking, temporal compression), not just a reshaped tensor.

---

**Undercomplete Autoencoder**

*The problem:* you have high-dimensional, unlabeled data and want the model to discover informative structure on its own, without supervision.

*Core insight / definition:* force the network to compress input $x \in \mathbb{R}^D$ through a narrow bottleneck $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \ll D$) via encoder $f_\phi$, then reconstruct via decoder $g_\theta$, minimizing $L = \|x - g_\theta(f_\phi(x))\|^2$ (or BCE for binary data). Accurate reconstruction through the bottleneck forces the model to capture the most important structure.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* if the bottleneck isn't tight enough, or the network has capacity to route information around it, the model learns a near-identity mapping with no meaningful compression — $d$ must be small enough to force true compression.

---

**Variational Autoencoder (VAE)**

*The problem:* a standard (deterministic) autoencoder maps each input to a single latent point, leaving gaps in latent space that decode to garbage when sampled.

*Core insight / definition:* map each input to a distribution (typically Gaussian) instead of a point: $q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \text{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x)))$, train the decoder $p_\theta(x|z)$ to reconstruct from samples of this distribution, and regularize toward a standard Gaussian prior via KL divergence in the ELBO objective. This densely covers the latent space so any sampled point decodes to something meaningful.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* VAE samples are blurrier than GAN/diffusion samples because the pixel-wise reconstruction loss (MSE/BCE) is a likelihood that, under a multimodal true output distribution, gets minimized by averaging over modes — this is a direct consequence of the objective, not a capacity limitation of the decoder.

---

**Vanishing Gradient (GAN failure mode)**

*The problem:* when the discriminator becomes too accurate too quickly, the generator receives essentially no useful learning signal.

*Core insight / definition:* when $D$ is near-perfect, $\log(1-D(G(z))) \approx 0$, so the generator's gradient approaches zero and it stops improving despite the discriminator's apparent success.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* fixed either locally via non-saturating loss (reformulate the generator objective) or structurally via WGAN's Lipschitz-constrained critic, which provides meaningful gradients even under non-overlapping distributions.

---

**Video Diffusion (as diffusion over time)**

*The problem:* extending image diffusion/flow matching to video introduces a temporal axis with its own consistency and compute challenges.

*Core insight / definition:* video generation is conceptually diffusion/flow matching plus a temporal axis; production systems address temporal consistency via temporal attention layers, control compute cost via spatial and temporal latent-space compression, and some systems use autoregressive-over-time hybrids (diffusing short windows conditioned on prior windows) trading long-range consistency for bounded compute.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* the per-step compute cost is already much higher than image generation (video is a 3D time×height×width tensor with attention cost growing sharply), so few-step sampling techniques matter proportionally more for video than for images.

---

**Wasserstein GAN (WGAN / WGAN-GP)**

*The problem:* standard GAN training suffers from vanishing gradients and oscillation, with no structural fix from loss reformulation alone.

*Core insight / definition:* replace the classifier discriminator with a critic that estimates the Earth-mover (Wasserstein) distance: $\mathcal{L}_\text{WGAN} = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_\text{data}}[D(x)] - \mathbb{E}_z[D(G(z))]$, with the critic constrained to be 1-Lipschitz (enforced via gradient penalty in WGAN-GP). This provides meaningful gradients even when generator and data distributions don't overlap at all.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* this is a structural solution to vanishing gradients, not a tuning trick — it changes the underlying divergence being optimized (Wasserstein distance instead of a JS/KL-like divergence).

---


## 09-reinforcement-learning

**Actor-Critic**

*The problem:* REINFORCE's Monte Carlo return has enormous variance and requires waiting for episode end, making learning slow and noisy.

*Core insight / definition:* Two networks work together: an actor $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ that picks actions, and a critic $V_\phi(s)$ that estimates state value via TD regression and supplies the baseline. The advantage becomes the TD error $\hat A_t = r_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)$, letting the actor update every step instead of waiting for the trajectory to end.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Learning the baseline (rather than estimating it from full returns) is what makes policy gradients practical at scale; GAE is the standard refinement that tunes the bias-variance dial of the advantage estimate.

---

**Advantage Function**

*The problem:* Raw returns or Q-values used as a policy-gradient weight carry variance from the state's baseline value, which has nothing to do with the action chosen.

*Core insight / definition:* $A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s)$ — how much better an action is than the policy's average behavior in that state. Subtracting $V(s)$ removes state-level noise, leaving a correctly-signed signal: positive means better than expected (reinforce), negative means worse (suppress).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* It is the variance-minimizing baseline choice and the central quantity policy gradient methods actually optimize against; a common trap is claiming baselines "reduce bias" — they reduce variance while leaving the expected gradient unchanged.

---

**AlphaGo / AlphaZero / MuZero**

*The problem:* A reactive policy network alone can't look ahead in games with deep tactics; and building a strong game AI historically required either human data or known rules.

*Core insight / definition:* AlphaGo combines a supervised policy (from human games), RL fine-tuning, and a value network to guide MCTS. AlphaZero drops human data entirely — pure self-play, one network outputs $(P, V)$, and MCTS acts as a policy-improvement operator whose search result becomes the next training target. MuZero removes even the rules: it learns a value-equivalent latent model (predicting only policy, value, and reward — not pixels) and plans inside that learned model.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* MCTS doesn't "make the network more accurate" — it produces a better policy at decision time by spending compute, and that output becomes the training signal; that self-improvement loop, not raw network capacity, is why AlphaZero has no human ceiling.

---

**Bandit (Multi-Armed / Contextual)**

*The problem:* You have $k$ options with noisy unknown rewards and no state — every trial spent learning about a bad option is reward forfeited, and interviewers use this to test whether you reach for the simplest sufficient tool instead of full RL.

*Core insight / definition:* The multi-armed bandit strips away states and transitions, leaving only repeated choices under uncertainty. A contextual bandit conditions the reward on context $x_t$ (learning $\mathbb{E}[r\mid x,a]$ instead of one mean per arm), turning "which option is best" into "which option is best for this user" — but remains one-step, since actions don't affect the next context.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* If the action doesn't change the next state, it's a bandit, not full RL — bandits are dramatically cheaper, safer, and more sample-efficient, and reaching for full RL when a bandit suffices is a flagged interview mistake.

---

**Baseline (in Policy Gradients)**

*The problem:* REINFORCE's gradient weight $G_t$ has huge variance, and if all returns are positive every sampled action gets reinforced regardless of quality.

*Core insight / definition:* Subtract any function of state $b(s)$ from the return: $\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)(G_t - b(s_t))]$. This stays unbiased for any action-independent $b(s)$ because $\mathbb{E}_a[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)]=0$; the variance-minimizing choice is $b(s)=V(s)$, turning the weight into the advantage.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* A baseline recenters the sign of the update so it carries real information ("better/worse than expected") rather than just magnitude; claiming it "speeds convergence" misses that it changes variance, not the expected gradient.

---

**Behavior Cloning (BC)**

*The problem:* Sometimes you have expert demonstrations but no reward function to run RL against.

*Core insight / definition:* Supervised learning that maps expert states directly to expert actions — no environment interaction needed. Its fatal flaw is **compounding error / covariate shift**: a small mistake moves the agent to a state the expert never visited, where errors are larger, so error grows quadratically ($O(\epsilon T^2)$) rather than linearly in horizon length.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* 99% training accuracy says nothing about deployment robustness, because errors aren't independent across steps — one drift changes the whole downstream distribution; LLM SFT is exactly behavior cloning and inherits the same ceiling.

---

**Bellman Equations (and Bellman Optimality Equation)**

*The problem:* Without a recursive structure, computing the value of a state would require enumerating every possible future trajectory.

*Core insight / definition:* $V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'} P(s'\mid s,a)[R(s,a)+\gamma V^\pi(s')]$ — the value of a state is immediate reward plus discounted value of the successor. The Bellman optimality equation replaces the policy average with a max: $Q^*(s,a) = \sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)[R(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')]$.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* The $\max$ is what makes the optimality equation nonlinear (and thus not solvable by direct linear algebra) — it's the entire difference between evaluating a policy and finding the best one, and every value-based algorithm approximates this equation from experience.

---

**Bootstrapping**

*The problem:* Waiting for an episode to end before learning anything (Monte Carlo) is slow, high-variance, and impossible on continuing tasks.

*Core insight / definition:* Update a value estimate using your own current estimate of the next state's value, rather than the true final return — "a guess from a guess." This is the core mechanism of TD learning, Q-learning, and DQN.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Bootstrapping is one leg of the deadly triad; combined with function approximation and off-policy data it can cause divergence, because an update that shifts many states' values can also shift the bootstrap target in the same direction, creating positive feedback.

---

**Contextual Bandit** — *see Bandit*

---

**Credit Assignment Problem**

*The problem:* In RL the reward for a decision may arrive many steps after the decision that caused it, unlike supervised learning where the label is immediate and direct.

*Core insight / definition:* The challenge of determining which of an agent's past actions is responsible for an observed outcome (reward). It is one of the two properties (along with policy-dependent data) that make RL harder than supervised learning.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Discounting, TD methods, and advantage estimation all exist partly to make credit assignment tractable; longer delays between action and reward generally require higher $\gamma$ and more sophisticated advantage estimators.

---

**Cumulative Regret**

*The problem:* You need a way to score a bandit algorithm's overall performance, not just its final estimate accuracy.

*Core insight / definition:* $\text{Regret}(T) = T\mu^* - \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}[r_t]$ — total reward lost relative to always having played the best arm. Linear regret $O(T)$ means the algorithm never stops making mistakes at a constant rate (failure); logarithmic regret $O(\log T)$ is the theoretical optimum (Lai–Robbins bound), achieved by UCB and Thompson Sampling.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Fixed-$\varepsilon$ greedy explores forever at a constant rate and therefore accrues linear regret no matter how confident it becomes — this is the formal reason it's "theoretically unsatisfying."

---

**CQL (Conservative Q-Learning) / IQL (Implicit Q-Learning)**

*The problem:* Naive offline Q-learning lets the Bellman max select the most overestimated out-of-distribution (OOD) action, and there's no environment feedback to correct the delusion.

*Core insight / definition:* CQL adds a regularizer that pushes Q-values down on OOD actions and up on in-data actions, learning a conservative lower bound. IQL never queries $Q$ at unseen actions at all — it uses expectile regression to approximate the max over in-support actions only, then extracts a policy via advantage-weighted regression.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Both implement the same underlying fix — "stay close to the data / be pessimistic about unseen actions" — IQL is the more common default for stability and simplicity; CQL when an explicit conservative value estimate is wanted.

---

**DAgger (Dataset Aggregation)**

*The problem:* Behavior cloning has no recovery behavior for states the expert never visited, since training data only covers the expert's own trajectory.

*Core insight / definition:* Iteratively run the current (learned) policy, have the expert label the states it actually visited, aggregate this into the training set, and retrain. This directly injects recovery behavior into the data, fixing covariate shift — but requires an interactive/queryable expert.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* More i.i.d. expert data doesn't fix BC's failure — DAgger works because it changes *which* states get labeled, not how much data there is.

---

**Deadly Triad**

*The problem:* DQN-style deep RL can mysteriously diverge — Q-values blow up — even though the algorithm looks like ordinary regression.

*Core insight / definition:* Divergence is guaranteed *possible* when all three of function approximation (neural net vs. table), bootstrapping (targets built from your own estimates), and off-policy learning (training data from a different policy than the one evaluated) are present simultaneously. Any two alone are safe. With a table, an update touches one entry; with a network, it shifts all states sharing features, and if that shift moves the bootstrap target in the same direction, you get runaway positive feedback.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* This is Sutton & Barto's framing and a frequent senior-level question; DQN's target network and replay buffer are mitigations, not solutions — they slow the feedback loop but don't eliminate it. Gradient-TD methods (GTD, TDC) are provably convergent but rarely used because they're slower and empirically weaker.

---

**Decision Transformer**

*The problem:* Offline RL's value-based approaches (CQL, IQL) still bootstrap and can suffer subtler extrapolation issues; is there a way to sidestep the value-function machinery entirely?

*Core insight / definition:* Treats a trajectory as a sequence `(return-to-go, state, action, ...)` and trains a Transformer to predict the next action conditioned on a desired return. At test time, condition on a high return-to-go. It's sequence modeling, not value iteration — no bootstrapping, hence no extrapolation blowup.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Because there's no max operator or bootstrapped target, the classic offline-RL overestimation failure mode structurally can't occur — a strong answer when asked "where does Decision Transformer sit" relative to CQL/IQL.

---

**DDPG / TD3 / SAC (Continuous-Control Family)**

*The problem:* Q-learning's $\arg\max_a$ requires enumerating actions, which is impossible for continuous action spaces (e.g., robot joint torques).

*Core insight / definition:* DDPG pairs a deterministic actor with a Q-critic, reusing DQN tricks for continuous actions. TD3 adds twin critics (taking the min, fixing overestimation) and delayed actor updates. SAC adds a maximum-entropy objective — maximizing return *and* policy entropy $\alpha\mathcal H(\pi(\cdot\mid s))$ — making exploration intrinsic.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* SAC is the usual default for continuous control: markedly less hyperparameter-sensitive than DDPG, and being off-policy it's far more sample-efficient than PPO — which matters when every sample is a real robot movement.

---

**Discount Factor (γ)**

*The problem:* An infinite sum of future rewards can diverge, and some notion of "sooner is better" needs to be built into the objective.

*Core insight / definition:* $\gamma \in [0,1]$ does three jobs: (1) mathematically guarantees the infinite return sum converges for bounded rewards when $\gamma<1$; (2) models genuine preference for sooner reward; (3) practically bounds the effective planning horizon to roughly $1/(1-\gamma)$ steps, controlling variance.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* γ is not a minor convergence knob — changing it can flip which policy is optimal entirely (a worked three-state example shows "stay" optimal at γ=0.9 but "go right" optimal at γ=0.5). A lower γ can also outperform in practice via lower variance/easier credit assignment, even if it isn't the "true" objective.

---

**Distributional Shift / Extrapolation Error**

*The problem:* Offline RL has no ability to test its beliefs about actions it hasn't seen, unlike online RL where exploration eventually corrects bad estimates.

*Core insight / definition:* The Bellman target's $\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$ takes a max over actions; for actions absent from the dataset, $Q$ is unconstrained, and the max systematically selects the most overestimated of these garbage values. The resulting policy prefers out-of-distribution actions precisely because the critic is delusional about them, with no environment feedback to correct it.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* This single idea is "the most important idea in offline RL" — it's why standard online tricks (vanilla DQN/SAC) don't transfer to fixed datasets, and why CQL/IQL/Decision Transformer all exist.

---

**DQN (Deep Q-Network)**

*The problem:* Tabular Q-learning needs one entry per state-action pair — impossible for high-dimensional inputs like images.

*Core insight / definition:* Replaces the Q-table with a neural network $Q_\theta(s,a)$, stabilized by three fixes: (1) **experience replay** — store transitions in a buffer and sample minibatches to break temporal correlation and reuse data; (2) **target network** — a frozen copy $\theta^-$ updated every $C$ steps (or via Polyak averaging) to prevent the bootstrap target from chasing the same parameters being updated; (3) **reward clipping/normalization** to keep gradients comparable in scale.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Naively training a Q-network without these fixes diverges. The target network fixes non-stationary targets, not overfitting — a commonly misattributed purpose; the replay buffer fixes sample correlation, a distinct problem, and both are needed together.

---

**Double DQN**

*The problem:* $\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$ over noisy estimates is systematically biased upward — overestimation bias — because whichever action happens to be overestimated is the one selected by the max.

*Core insight / definition:* Decouples action selection from evaluation: the online network selects the action ($\arg\max_{a'}Q_\theta(s',a')$), and the target network evaluates it ($Q_{\theta^-}$). An action overestimated by one network is unlikely to be equally overestimated by the independent other.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* This is close to a free fix (minimal implementation cost) and is usually the first thing to try if Q-values are exploding; the mechanism (Jensen's inequality: $\mathbb{E}[\max_a\hat Q]\geq\max_a\mathbb{E}[\hat Q]$) is worth stating precisely in interviews.

---

**Dueling DQN**

*The problem:* In many states, the identity of the action barely matters to the outcome, so learning a full per-action Q-value everywhere wastes network capacity.

*Core insight / definition:* Splits the network into separate $V(s)$ and $A(s,a)$ streams that are recombined to produce $Q(s,a)$, letting the network share representation for state value across all actions.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* One of the component improvements folded into Rainbow; useful whenever action choice has little effect on many states.

---

**Dyna / World Models (Dreamer) / Model-Based RL**

*The problem:* Real environment interaction can be the dominant cost (physics sims, real robots); learning purely model-free wastes every real step on a single gradient update.

*Core insight / definition:* Model-based RL learns dynamics $\hat P(s'\mid s,a)$ (and reward), then uses it to generate synthetic experience. **Dyna** interleaves updates from real and imagined transitions sampled from the learned model. **World models / Dreamer** learn dynamics in a compact latent space and train the policy purely on latent rollouts ("dreams"), touching the real environment only to collect data — currently the sample-efficiency frontier.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* The universal risk is **model exploitation / compounding error** — the policy finds and exploits inaccuracies in the learned model, and one-step errors compound over a rollout; mitigations include short rollouts, model ensembles for uncertainty, and penalizing reward in high-uncertainty regions.

---

**ε-Greedy**

*The problem:* You need the simplest possible rule for balancing exploration and exploitation in a bandit or RL setting.

*Core insight / definition:* With probability $\varepsilon$, pick an action uniformly at random (explore); otherwise pick the current best-estimated action (exploit). Trivial to implement, but exploration is *undirected* — as likely to retry a known-bad arm as an unknown one.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* With fixed $\varepsilon$ it explores forever at a constant rate and accrues linear regret; decaying $\varepsilon_t \propto 1/t$ recovers logarithmic regret while staying trivial to implement.

---

**Exploration–Exploitation Trade-off**

*The problem:* An agent must both discover which actions are good (explore) and capitalize on what it currently believes is best (exploit), and every trial spent on one is a trial not spent on the other.

*Core insight / definition:* Pure exploitation risks locking onto an option that only looked good by chance (thin evidence); pure exploration wastes trials on options already known to be poor. Good algorithms explore in proportion to uncertainty, not at a fixed rate.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Framing exploration as "a cost, not a setting" — every exploratory action is a deliberately suboptimal one — is exactly what interviewers probe for; justifying that spend (e.g., can you afford it on live users?) is often the real question.

---

**GAE (Generalized Advantage Estimation)**

*The problem:* The one-step TD advantage is low variance but biased; the full Monte Carlo advantage is unbiased but high variance — you need a way to trade off between them.

*Core insight / definition:* Interpolates across $n$-step advantage estimates with a decay parameter $\lambda$: $\lambda=0$ gives the one-step TD advantage (low variance, biased), $\lambda=1$ recovers Monte Carlo (unbiased, high variance). $\lambda \approx 0.95$ is the standard default.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* GAE is the practical mechanism actor-critic and PPO implementations actually use to compute $\hat A_t$ — treating it as a fixed formula rather than a bias-variance dial misses the point.

---

**GAIL (Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning) / Inverse RL**

*The problem:* Cloning actions pointwise doesn't generalize to states the expert never visited; sometimes you want to recover the underlying intent, not just mimic behavior.

*Core insight / definition:* Inverse RL infers the reward function the expert appears to optimize, then runs RL on it — reward transfers across dynamics better than actions do, but IRL is expensive and underdetermined. GAIL is the practical modern form: a GAN-style setup where a discriminator learns to distinguish agent from expert trajectories, and the policy is trained to fool it — imitation without ever explicitly recovering a reward.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* GAIL matches the expert's *state-visitation distribution* rather than pointwise actions, which generalizes far better to states not exactly in the demonstration set.

---

**GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization)**

*The problem:* PPO for RLHF needs a learned value function (critic) for the advantage estimate, and at LLM scale that critic roughly doubles training memory and compute.

*Core insight / definition:* For each prompt, sample a group of $G$ completions from the current policy, score each with a reward model or rule-based verifier, and compute advantage as the group z-score: $\hat A_i = (r_i - \text{mean}(r_1,\ldots,r_G))/\text{std}(r_1,\ldots,r_G)$. This group-relative baseline replaces the value network entirely; the rest reuses PPO's clipped surrogate objective plus an explicit KL penalty to a reference policy.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* GRPO trades more rollout compute per update (needs multiple samples per prompt) for no critic training, and wins specifically when rollouts are cheap and verifiable (math/code) relative to critic cost — which is why it appears in reasoning-model post-training (DeepSeek-Math, DeepSeek-R1).

---

**Imitation Learning**

*The problem:* Sometimes there is no reward function to specify at all, but expert demonstrations exist.

*Core insight / definition:* An umbrella family that recovers a policy (or reward) from demonstrations rather than reward signals: behavior cloning (direct supervised mapping), DAgger (iterative aggregation with expert labels), and inverse RL/GAIL (recover or match on the reward/state-distribution level).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Imitation is capped by the expert — it cannot exceed demonstrated behavior and faithfully copies the expert's mistakes and biases; LLM SFT is behavior cloning, and RLHF is what's layered on top to go beyond imitation.

---

**Markov Decision Process (MDP)**

*The problem:* RL needs a formal container that specifies states, actions, dynamics, rewards, and the value of the future, so algorithms can be defined and compared precisely.

*Core insight / definition:* The tuple $(\mathcal S, \mathcal A, P, R, \gamma)$: state space, action space, transition dynamics $P(s'\mid s,a)$, reward function $R(s,a)$, and discount factor $\gamma$. Built on the **Markov property** — the future depends only on the current state, not the history: $P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t) = P(s_{t+1}\mid s_1,a_1,\ldots,s_t,a_t)$.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* The Markov property is an assumption about your *state representation*, not the world — calling a problem "non-Markovian" as a fixed property of the environment is a common trap; almost any process can be made Markovian by enriching the state (e.g., stacking frames to recover velocity).

---

**MCTS (Monte Carlo Tree Search) / UCT / PUCT**

*The problem:* A feedforward policy picks only the locally-good action; in games with deep tactics you need to look ahead and simulate consequences before committing.

*Core insight / definition:* Builds a search tree via four repeated phases: **selection** (descend via UCT/PUCT, balancing $Q$ against exploration $\propto P(a)\sqrt{N_{\text{parent}}}/(1+N)$), **expansion** (add a leaf), **evaluation** (estimate leaf value via rollout or value network), **backup** (propagate value up the path, updating $Q$ and visit counts $N$). Act by the most-visited child, then reuse the subtree.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Visit count, not raw value, is used to pick the final move because it's a robust low-variance signal — a single high $Q$ can be a noisy leaf estimate. UCT is explicitly the bandit UCB idea (optimism under uncertainty) applied at each tree node.

---

**MuZero** — *see AlphaGo / AlphaZero / MuZero*

---

**Non-Stationarity (in Bandits)**

*The problem:* Standard bandit algorithms assume each arm's reward distribution is fixed forever, but real arms (ads, content) decay in quality over time (e.g., ad fatigue).

*Core insight / definition:* Without discounting, an arm's early success dominates its running mean average forever, so recent poor performance barely shifts the estimate — the algorithm keeps exploiting a once-good arm long past its actual decline. Mitigations: sliding windows, discounting old observations, periodic posterior resets, or adding "age" as a context feature.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* This is the single most common production bandit failure; swapping UCB for Thompson Sampling does *not* fix it — every standard bandit shares the stationarity assumption, only *discounted* variants address it.

---

**Off-Policy vs. On-Policy Learning**

*The problem:* You need to distinguish whether an algorithm can learn about a policy different from the one generating its data, since this determines whether replay buffers and logged data can be used.

*Core insight / definition:* **Off-policy** algorithms (Q-learning, DQN, SAC, DDPG) learn about the greedy/target policy regardless of the behavior policy generating the data — enabled by the $\max$ in the Bellman target. **On-policy** algorithms (SARSA, PPO, vanilla policy gradient) must learn the value of, and use data from, the policy currently being executed, and must discard data after each update.

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* Off-policy learning is one leg of the deadly triad and is what permits replay buffers and learning from logged data; on cliff-walking, Q-learning (off-policy) learns the risky optimal path while SARSA (on-policy) learns a safer path because its target accounts for the exploring policy's chance of stepping off the cliff.

---

**Offline RL**

*The problem:* Many real domains (healthcare, autonomous driving, recommendation) forbid or make dangerous the live exploration that online RL needs — you only have logged data and cannot collect more on-policy.

*Core insight / definition:* Learns a policy entirely from a fixed dataset $\mathcal D=\{(s,a,r,s')\}$ collected by a behavior policy $\pi_\beta$, with no new environment interaction. The defining challenge is distributional shift/extrapolation error; the standard fix shape is to stay close to the data / be pessimistic about unseen actions (CQL, IQL, Decision Transformer).

*Why it matters / pitfall / interview trap:* The further the learned policy strays from $\pi_\beta$, the less trustworthy both the policy and its offline evaluation become; no algorithm can conjure a great policy from data generated by one narrow, mediocre behavior policy — offline RL cannot escape the support of its data.

---

**Off-Policy Evaluation (OPE) / Importance Sampling**
